## Introduction

We will run a *targets* pipeline that reads a specified
`HealthWellbeing` version, pools the study correlations, and writes a
summary for the report. By the end of these 18 minutes, you should be
able to trace the summary back to its input and predict what rebuilds
when you select another version.

You need *box*, *pins*, *targets*, and *meta* in your workshop R
environment. The dependency graph also uses *visNetwork*. Start with
the local board and version selection file from the previous lesson.
Your instructor can share a prepared board and summary for comparison.
[Dataset storage and versioning](05_pins.qmd#pins-checkpoint)

## Inspect the pipeline

The script is `pipelines/_targets_health_wellbeing.R`. Open it in your
editor and follow the data dependencies in this order.

```text
version_file -> data_version -> dataset_file -> studies -> fit
fit, data_version, and code_revision_file -> result -> summary_file
```

We mark the selector, pinned RDS, revision text, and summary CSV as
file targets. This lets *targets* track those files as the pipeline
runs. The code revision records the checkout used for analysis.
Commit any edits you want represented by the revision before recording
it.

The model uses the raw Pearson correlations and study sample sizes.
*Meta* transforms each correlation to Fisher's z scale and pools
the effects with a random-effects model. We use restricted maximum
likelihood (REML) to estimate between-study variance and the
Hartung–Knapp method for the 95% interval. The summary converts the
estimate and limits back to the correlation scale.

This model treats study summaries as independent and assumes their
correlations address a comparable association. Differences in
populations, measures, and sampling limit interpretation. This is a
worked example of pooling reported effects from the supplied studies.
[Section 4.2.4 of the guide](https://doing-meta.guide/pooling-es#correlations)

## Run the full dataset

From the project root, record the Git revision in the Terminal.

```bash
git rev-parse HEAD > outputs/health-wellbeing/code-revision.txt
```

In the R Console, load the commands used to inspect and run the
pipeline. The store path keeps this exercise's cache separate from
other pipelines.

```{r health-targets-setup, cache = FALSE}
box::use(
  targets[tar_make, tar_outdated, tar_read, tar_visnetwork],
  utils[read.csv]
)

workshop_dir <- file.path("outputs", "health-wellbeing")
pipeline_script <- file.path("pipelines", "_targets_health_wellbeing.R")
pipeline_store <- file.path(workshop_dir, "_targets")
selection_file <- file.path(workshop_dir, "analysis-data-version.txt")
```

Use the graph to predict which targets depend on the selector. If
you're using the PDF, follow the text diagram above.

```{r health-targets-graph, cache = FALSE}
tar_visnetwork(
  script = pipeline_script,
  store = pipeline_store,
  targets_only = TRUE,
  outdated = FALSE
)
```

We will build the targets and inspect the cached result.

```{r health-targets-run, cache = FALSE}
tar_make(script = pipeline_script, store = pipeline_store)
tar_read(result, store = pipeline_store)
```

## Try it yourself

Change the selector from all studies to the 18 general-population
studies. Predict which branches of the graph are affected, then ask
*targets* which targets are outdated and rebuild.

```{r health-targets-change-input, cache = FALSE}
versions <- read.csv(
  file.path(workshop_dir, "dataset-versions.csv"),
  colClasses = "character"
)
general_version <- versions$version[versions$scope == "general"]
stopifnot(length(general_version) == 1L)
writeLines(general_version, selection_file)

tar_outdated(script = pipeline_script, store = pipeline_store)
tar_make(script = pipeline_script, store = pipeline_store)
tar_read(result, store = pipeline_store)
```

Compare the study count and pooled correlation with the first run.
The changed input is a planned teaching subset. The difference
reflects which studies entered the model, including any differences
in study precision and heterogeneity.

Switch back to the full version for the reporting activity so everyone
can compare with the same example.

```{r health-targets-restore-full, cache = FALSE}
full_version <- versions$version[versions$scope == "all"]
stopifnot(length(full_version) == 1L)
writeLines(full_version, selection_file)
tar_make(script = pipeline_script, store = pipeline_store)
tar_outdated(script = pipeline_script, store = pipeline_store)
```

## Checkpoint {#targets-checkpoint}

The full example combines **29 studies** with a pooled correlation of
about **0.36** and a 95% interval of about **0.31 to 0.41**. The
alternative input combines **18 studies**. The selector and downstream
analysis rebuild when it changes. The code revision file has the same
content across both runs. After restoring the full selection and
rebuilding, `tar_outdated()` should be empty.

The file `outputs/health-wellbeing/meta-summary.csv` now contains the
full result. The fit stores the R and *meta* versions used to create
it. The report keeps those versions when the pipeline reuses a fit.
Use a clean pipeline store to check results in a changed environment.
[Reproducible reporting and publishing](07_quarto.qmd)
